{{Short description|Mathematical relation defining a sequence}}
{{further|Constant-recursive sequence}}

In [[mathematics]] (including [[combinatorics]], [[linear algebra]], and [[dynamical systems]]), a '''linear recurrence with constant coefficients'''<ref name=Chiang>{{cite book |last=Chiang |first=Alpha |title=Fundamental Methods of Mathematical Economics |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalmetho0000chia_h4v2 |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=McGraw-Hill |edition=Third |year=1984 |isbn=0-07-010813-7 }}</ref>{{rp|at=ch. 17}}<ref name=Baumol>{{cite book |last=Baumol |first=William |authorlink=William Baumol |title=Economic Dynamics |url=https://archive.org/details/economicdynamics0000baum_c7i2 |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=Macmillan |edition=Third |year=1970 |isbn=0-02-306660-1 }}</ref>{{rp|at=ch. 10}} (also known as a '''linear recurrence relation''' or '''linear difference equation''') sets equal to 0 a [[polynomial]] that is linear in the various iterates of a [[variable (mathematics)|variable]]—that is, in the values of the elements of a [[sequence]]. The polynomial's linearity means that each of its terms has [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] 0 or 1. A linear recurrence denotes the evolution of some variable over time, with the current [[discrete time|time period]] or discrete moment in time denoted as {{mvar|t}}, one period earlier denoted as {{math|''t'' − 1}}, one period later as {{math|''t'' + 1}}, etc.

The ''[[equation solving|solution]]'' of such an equation is a function of {{mvar|t}}, and not of any iterate values, giving the value of the iterate at any time. To find the solution it is necessary to know the specific values (known as ''[[initial condition]]s'') of {{mvar|n}} of the iterates, and normally these are the {{mvar|n}} iterates that are oldest. The equation or its variable is said to be ''[[Lyapunov stability#Definition for discrete-time systems|stable]]'' if from any set of initial conditions the variable's limit as time goes to infinity exists; this limit is called the ''[[steady state]]''.

Difference equations are used in a variety of contexts, such as in [[economics]] to model the evolution through time of variables such as [[gross domestic product]], the [[inflation rate]], the [[exchange rate]], etc. They are used in modeling such [[time series]] because values of these variables are only measured at discrete intervals. In [[econometrics|econometric]] applications, linear difference equations are modeled with [[stochastic process|stochastic terms]] in the form of [[autoregressive model|autoregressive (AR) model]]s and in models such as [[vector autoregression]] (VAR) and [[autoregressive moving average]] (ARMA) models that combine AR with other features.

==Definitions==

A '''linear recurrence with constant coefficients''' is an equation of the following form, written in terms of [[parameter#Mathematical functions|parameters]] {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''a''<sub>''n''</sub>}} and {{mvar|b}}:

<math display="block">y_t = a_1y_{t-1} + \cdots + a_ny_{t-n} + b,</math>

or equivalently as

<math display="block">y_{t+n}= a_1y_{t+n-1} + \cdots + a_ny_t + b.</math>

The positive integer <math>n</math> is called the '''order''' of the recurrence and denotes the longest time lag between iterates. The equation is called '''homogeneous''' if {{math|1=''b'' = 0}} and '''nonhomogeneous''' if {{math|''b'' ≠ 0}}.

If the equation is homogeneous, the coefficients determine the '''[[characteristic polynomial]]''' (also "auxiliary polynomial" or "companion polynomial")

<math display="block">p(\lambda)= \lambda^n - a_1\lambda^{n-1} - a_2\lambda^{n-2}-\cdots-a_{n}</math>

whose roots play a crucial role in finding and understanding the sequences satisfying the recurrence.

==Conversion to homogeneous form==

If {{math|''b'' ≠ 0}}, the equation

<math display="block">y_t = a_1y_{t-1} + \cdots + a_ny_{t-n} + b</math>

is said to be ''nonhomogeneous''. To solve this equation it is convenient to convert it to homogeneous form, with no [[constant term]]. This is done by first finding the equation's ''steady state value''—a value {{math|''y''*}} such that, if {{mvar|n}} successive iterates all had this value, so would all future values. This value is found by setting all values of {{mvar|y}} equal to {{math|''y''*}} in the difference equation, and solving, thus obtaining

<math display="block">y^* = \frac{b}{1-a_1-\cdots - a_n}</math>

assuming the denominator is not 0. If it is zero, the steady state does not exist.

Given the steady state, the difference equation can be rewritten in terms of deviations of the iterates from the steady state, as

<math display="block">\left(y_t -y^*\right)= a_1\left(y_{t-1}-y^*\right) + \cdots + a_n\left(y_{t-n}-y^*\right)</math>

which has no constant term, and which can be written more succinctly as

<math display="block">x_t= a_1x_{t-1} + \cdots + a_nx_{t-n} </math>

where {{mvar|x}} equals {{math|''y'' − ''y''*}}. This is the homogeneous form.

If there is no steady state, the difference equation

<math display="block">y_t = a_1y_{t-1} + \cdots + a_ny_{t-n} + b</math>

can be combined with its equivalent form

<math display="block">y_{t-1}= a_1y_{t-2}+ \cdots + a_ny_{t-(n+1)}+ b</math>

to obtain (by solving both for {{mvar|b}})

<math display="block">y_t - a_1y_{t-1} - \cdots - a_ny_{t-n} = y_{t-1}- a_1y_{t-2}- \cdots - a_ny_{t-(n+1)}</math>

in which [[like terms]] can be combined to give a homogeneous equation of one order higher than the original.

==Solution example for small orders==

The roots of the characteristic polynomial play a crucial role in finding and understanding the sequences satisfying the recurrence. If there are <math>d</math> distinct roots <math>r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_d,</math>  then each solution to the recurrence takes the form
<math display="block">a_n = k_1 r_1^n + k_2 r_2^n + \cdots + k_d r_d^n,</math>
where the coefficients <math>k_i</math> are determined in order to fit the initial conditions of the recurrence. When the same roots occur multiple times, the terms in this formula corresponding to the second and later occurrences of the same root are multiplied by increasing powers of <math>n</math>. For instance, if the characteristic polynomial can be factored as <math>(x-r)^3</math>, with the same root <math>r</math> occurring three times, then the solution would take the form
<math display="block">a_n = k_1 r^n + k_2 n r^n + k_3 n^2 r^n.</math><ref>{{citation|contribution=2.1.1 Constant coefficients – A) Homogeneous equations|title=Mathematics for the Analysis of Algorithms|first1=Daniel H.|last1=Greene | first2=Donald E.|last2=Knuth | author2-link=Donald Knuth| edition=2nd| publisher=Birkhäuser |page=17 | year=1982}}.</ref>

===Order 1===

For order 1, the recurrence
<math display="block">a_{n}=r a_{n-1}</math>
has the solution <math>a_n = r^n</math> with <math>a_0 = 1</math> and the most general solution is <math>a_n = k r^n</math> with <math>a_0 = k</math>. The  characteristic polynomial equated to zero (the [[Characteristic polynomial|characteristic equation]]) is simply <math>t - r = 0</math>.

===Order 2===

Solutions to such recurrence relations of higher order are found by systematic means, often using the fact that <math>a_n = r^n</math> is a solution for the recurrence exactly when <math>t = r</math> is a root of the characteristic polynomial. This can be approached directly or using [[generating function]]s ([[formal power series]]) or matrices.

Consider, for example, a recurrence relation of the form
<math display="block">a_{n} = Aa_{n-1}+Ba_{n-2}.</math>

When does it have a solution of the same general form as <math>a_n = r^n</math>? Substituting this guess ([[ansatz]]) in the recurrence relation, we find that
<math display="block">r^{n}=Ar^{n-1}+Br^{n-2}</math>
must be true for '''all''' <math>n > 1</math>.

Dividing through by <math>r^{n-2}</math>, we get that all these equations reduce to the same statement:

<math display="block">\begin{align} r^2 &= Ar + B, \\ r^2 - Ar - B &= 0, \end{align}</math>

which is the characteristic equation of the recurrence relation.  Solve for <math>r</math> to obtain the two roots <math>\lambda_1</math>, <math>\lambda_2</math>: these roots are known as the [[characteristic root]]s or '''eigenvalues''' of the characteristic equation. The form of the solutions depends on the nature of these roots: If the roots are distinct, we have the general solution

<math display="block">a_n = C\lambda_1^n+D\lambda_2^n</math>

while if they are identical (when <math>A^2 + 4 B = 0</math>), we have

<math display="block">a_n = C\lambda^n + D n\lambda^n</math>

This is the most general solution; the two constants <math>C</math> and <math>D</math> can be chosen based on two given initial conditions <math>a_0</math> and <math>a_1</math> to produce a specific solution.

In the case of complex eigenvalues (which also gives rise to complex values for the solution parameters <math>C</math> and <math>D</math>), the use of complex numbers can be eliminated by rewriting the solution in trigonometric form.  In this case we can write the eigenvalues as <math>\lambda_1, \lambda_2 = \alpha \pm \beta i.</math> Then it can be shown that

<math display="block">a_n = C\lambda_1^n + D\lambda_2^n</math>

can be rewritten as<ref>Chiang, Alpha C., ''Fundamental Methods of Mathematical Economics'', third edition, McGraw-Hill, 1984.</ref>{{rp|pp=576–585}}

<math display="block">a_n = 2 M^n \left( E \cos(\theta n) + F \sin(\theta n)\right) = 2 G M^n \cos(\theta n - \delta),</math>

where

<math display="block">\begin{array}{lcl}
  M = \sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2} & \cos (\theta) =\tfrac{\alpha}{M} & \sin( \theta) = \tfrac{\beta}{M} \\
  C,D = E \mp F i & & \\
  G = \sqrt{E^2+F^2} & \cos (\delta ) = \tfrac{E}{G} & \sin (\delta )= \tfrac{F}{G}
\end{array}</math>

Here <math>E</math> and <math>F</math> (or equivalently, <math>G</math> and <math>\delta</math>)  are real constants which depend on the initial conditions. Using 
<math display="block">\lambda_1+\lambda_2=2 \alpha = A,</math>
<math display="block">\lambda_1 \cdot \lambda_2=\alpha^2+\beta^2=-B,</math>

one may simplify the solution given above as

<math display="block">a_n = (-B)^{\frac{n}{2}} \left( E \cos(\theta n) + F \sin(\theta n)\right),</math>

where <math>a_1</math> and <math>a_2</math> are the initial conditions and

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 E &= \frac{-A a_1 + a_2}{B} \\
 F &=-i \frac{A^2 a_1 - A a_2 +2 a_1 B}{B \sqrt{A^2+4B}} \\
\theta &=\arccos \left (\frac{A}{2 \sqrt{-B}} \right )
\end{align}</math>

In this way there is no need to solve for <math>\lambda_1</math> and <math>\lambda_2</math>.

In all cases—real distinct eigenvalues, real duplicated eigenvalues, and complex conjugate eigenvalues—the equation is [[stability theory|stable]] (that is, the variable <math>a</math> converges to a fixed value [specifically, zero]) [[if and only if]] ''both'' eigenvalues are smaller than one in [[absolute value]].  In this second-order case, this condition on the eigenvalues can be shown<ref>Papanicolaou, Vassilis, "On the asymptotic stability of a class of linear difference equations," ''Mathematics Magazine'' 69(1), February 1996, 34&ndash;43.</ref> to be equivalent to <math>|A| < 1 - B < 2</math>, which is equivalent to <math>|B| < 1</math> and <math>|A| < 1 - B</math>.

==General solution==
===Characteristic polynomial and roots===
Solving the homogeneous equation

<math display="block">x_t= a_1x_{t-1} + \cdots + a_nx_{t-n} </math>

involves first solving its characteristic polynomial

<math display="block">\lambda^n = a_1\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots + a_{n-2}\lambda^2+a_{n-1} \lambda + a_n</math>

for its characteristic roots {{math|''λ''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''λ''<sub>''n''</sub>}}. These roots can be solved for [[algebraic expression|algebraically]] if {{math|''n'' ≤ 4}}, but [[Abel–Ruffini theorem|not necessarily otherwise]]. If the solution is to be used numerically, all the roots of this characteristic equation can be found by [[numerical methods]]. However, for use in a theoretical context it may be that the only information required about the roots is whether any of them are greater than or equal to 1 in [[absolute value]].

It may be that all the roots are [[real number|real]] or instead there may be some that are [[complex number]]s. In the latter case, all the complex roots come in [[complex conjugate]] pairs.

===Solution with distinct characteristic roots===
If all the characteristic roots are distinct, the solution of the homogeneous linear recurrence

<math display="block">x_t= a_1x_{t-1} + \cdots + a_nx_{t-n} </math>

can be written in terms of the characteristic roots as

<math display="block">x_t=c_1\lambda_1^t +\cdots + c_n\lambda_n^t</math>

where the coefficients {{math|''c''<sub>''i''</sub>}} can be found by invoking the initial conditions. Specifically, for each time period for which an iterate value is known, this value and its corresponding value of {{mvar|t}} can be substituted into the solution equation to obtain a linear equation in the {{mvar|n}} as-yet-unknown parameters; {{mvar|n}} such equations, one for each initial condition, can be [[system of linear equations|solved simultaneously]] for the {{mvar|n}} parameter values. If all characteristic roots are real, then all the coefficient values {{math|''c''<sub>''i''</sub>}} will also be real; but with non-real complex roots, in general some of these coefficients will also be non-real.

====Converting complex solution to trigonometric form====

If there are complex roots, they come in conjugate pairs and so do the complex terms in the solution equation. If two of these complex terms are {{math|''c''<sub>''j''</sub>''λ''{{su|b=''j''|p=''t''}}}} and {{math|''c''<sub>''j''+1</sub>''λ''{{su|b=''j''+1|p=''t''}}}}, the roots {{math|''λ''<sub>''j''</sub>}} can be written as

<math display="block">\lambda_j, \lambda_{j+1}=\alpha \pm \beta i =M\left(\frac{\alpha}{M} \pm \frac{\beta}{M}i\right) </math>

where {{mvar|i}} is the [[imaginary unit]] and {{mvar|M}} is the [[absolute value|modulus]] of the roots:

<math display="block">M = \sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2}.</math>

Then the two complex terms in the solution equation can be written as

<math display="block">\begin{align}
c_j\lambda_j^t + c_{j+1}\lambda_{j+1}^t
& = M^t\left(c_j\left(\frac{\alpha}{M} + \frac{\beta}{M}i\right)^t + c_{j+1}\left(\frac{\alpha}{M} - \frac{\beta}{M}i\right)^t\right) \\[6pt]
& = M^t\left(c_j\left(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta\right)^t + c_{j+1}\left(\cos \theta - i\sin\theta\right)^t\right) \\[6pt]
& = M^t\bigl(c_j\left(\cos\theta t + i\sin \theta t\right) + c_{j+1}\left(\cos\theta t - i\sin\theta t\right) \bigr)
\end{align}</math>

where {{mvar|θ}} is the angle whose cosine is {{math|{{sfrac|''α''|''M''}}}} and whose sine is {{math|{{sfrac|''β''|''M''}}}}; the last equality here made use of [[de Moivre's formula]].

Now the process of finding the coefficients {{math|''c''<sub>''j''</sub>}} and {{math|''c''<sub>''j''+1</sub>}} guarantees that they are also complex conjugates, which can be written as {{math|''γ'' ± ''δi''}}. Using this in the last equation gives this expression for the two complex terms in the solution equation:

<math display="block">2M^t\left(\gamma \cos\theta t - \delta \sin\theta t\right)</math>

which can also be written as

<math display="block">2\sqrt{\gamma^2+\delta^2}M^t \cos(\theta t + \psi)</math>

where {{mvar|ψ}} is the angle whose cosine is {{math|{{sfrac|''γ''|{{sqrt|''γ''<sup>2</sup> + ''δ''<sup>2</sup>}}}}}} and whose sine is {{math|{{sfrac|''δ''|{{sqrt|''γ''<sup>2</sup> + ''δ''<sup>2</sup>}}}}}}.

====Cyclicity====
Depending on the initial conditions, even with all roots real the iterates can experience a transitory tendency to go above and below the steady state value. But true cyclicity involves a permanent tendency to fluctuate, and this occurs if there is at least one pair of complex conjugate characteristic roots. This can be seen in the trigonometric form of their contribution to the solution equation, involving {{math|cos&thinsp;''θt''}} and {{math|sin&thinsp;''θt''}}.

===Solution with duplicate characteristic roots===
In the second-order case, if the two roots are identical ({{math|1=''λ''<sub>1</sub> = ''λ''<sub>2</sub>}}), they can both be denoted as {{mvar|λ}} and a solution may be of the form

<math display="block">x_t = c_1 \lambda^t + c_2 t \lambda^t.</math>

===Solution by conversion to matrix form===
An alternative solution method involves converting the {{mvar|n}}th order difference equation to a first-order [[matrix difference equation]]. This is accomplished by writing {{math|1=''w''<sub>1,''t''</sub> = ''y''<sub>''t''</sub>}}, {{math|1=''w''<sub>2,''t''</sub> = ''y''<sub>''t''−1</sub> = ''w''<sub>1,''t''−1</sub>}}, {{math|1=''w''<sub>3,''t''</sub> = ''y''<sub>''t''−2</sub> = ''w''<sub>2,''t''−1</sub>}}, and so on. Then the original single {{mvar|n}}th-order equation

<math display="block">y_t = a_1y_{t-1} + a_2y_{t-2} + \cdots + a_ny_{t-n} + b</math>

can be replaced by the following {{mvar|n}} first-order equations:

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
w_{1, t} & = a_1w_{1, t-1} + a_2w_{2, t-1}+\cdots + a_nw_{n, t-1} + b \\
w_{2, t} & = w_{1, t-1} \\
& \,\,\,\vdots \\
w_{n,t} & =w_{n-1, t-1}.
\end{align}
</math>

Defining the vector {{math|'''w'''<sub>''i''</sub>}} as

<math display="block">\mathbf{w}_i = \begin{bmatrix}w_{1,i} \\ w_{2,i} \\ \vdots \\ w_{n,i} \end{bmatrix}</math>

this can be put in matrix form as

<math display="block">\mathbf{w}_t = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}</math>

Here {{math|'''A'''}} is an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix in which the first row contains {{math|''a''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''a''<sub>''n''</sub>}} and all other rows have a single 1 with all other elements being 0, and {{math|'''b'''}} is a column vector with first element {{mvar|b}} and with the rest of its elements being 0.

This matrix equation can be solved using the methods in the article [[Matrix difference equation]].
In the homogeneous case {{math|y<sub>i</sub>}} is a para-permanent of a lower [[triangular matrix]]<ref>{{cite journal| journal=J. Int. Seq.| first1=Roman|last1=Zatorsky| first2=Taras|last2=Goy| year=2016| volume=19| pages=16.2.2| title=Parapermanent of triangular matrices and some general theorems on number sequences | url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL19/Goy/goy2.html}}</ref>

===Solution using generating functions===

The recurrence

<math display="block">y_t = a_1y_{t-1} + \cdots + a_ny_{t-n} + b,</math>

can be solved using the theory of [[generating function]]s. First, we write <math display="inline">Y(x) = \sum_{t \ge 0} y_t x^t</math>. The recurrence is then equivalent to the following generating function equation:

<math display="block">Y(x) = a_1xY(x) + a_2x^2Y(x) + \cdots + a_nx^nY(x) + \frac{b}{1-x} + p(x)</math>

where <math>p(x)</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>n-1</math> correcting the initial terms.
From this equation we can solve to get

<math display="block">Y(x) = \left(\frac{b}{1-x} + p(x)\right) \cdot \frac{1}{1 - a_1 x - a_2 x^2 - \cdots - a_n x^n}.</math>

In other words, not worrying about the exact coefficients, <math>Y(x)</math> can be expressed as a [[rational function]] <math>Y(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.</math>

The closed form can then be derived via [[partial fraction decomposition]]. Specifically, if the generating function is written as
<math display="block">\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \sum_i \frac{f_i(x)}{(x - r_i)^{m_i}} </math>

then the polynomial <math>p(x)</math> determines the initial set of corrections <math>z(n)</math>, the denominator <math>(x - r_i)^m</math> determines the exponential term <math>r_i^n</math>, and the degree <math>m</math> together with the numerator <math>f_i(x)</math> determine the polynomial coefficient <math>k_i(n)</math>.

===Relation to solution to differential equations===

The method for solving linear [[differential equations]] is similar to the method above—the "intelligent guess" ([[ansatz]]) for linear differential equations with constant coefficients is <math>e^{\lambda x}</math> where <math>\lambda</math> is a complex number that is determined by substituting the guess into the differential equation.

This is not a coincidence.  Considering the [[Taylor series]] of the solution to a linear differential equation:

<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^\infin \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n</math>

it can be seen that the coefficients of the series are given by the <math>n</math>-th derivative of <math>f(x)</math> evaluated at the point <math>a</math>. The differential equation provides a linear difference equation relating these coefficients.

This equivalence can be used to quickly solve for the recurrence relationship for the coefficients in the power series solution of a linear differential equation.

The rule of thumb (for equations in which the polynomial multiplying the first term is non-zero at zero) is that:

<math display="block">y^{[k]} \to  f[n+k]</math>
and more generally
<math display="block">x^m*y^{[k]} \to n(n-1)...(n-m+1)f[n+k-m]</math>

'''Example:''' The recurrence relationship for the Taylor series coefficients of the equation:

<math display="block"> (x^2 + 3x -4)y^{[3]} -(3x+1)y^{[2]} + 2y = 0</math>

is given by

<math display="block"> n(n-1)f[n+1] + 3nf[n+2] -4f[n+3] -3nf[n+1] -f[n+2]+ 2f[n] = 0</math>

or

<math display="block">-4f[n+3] +2nf[n+2] + n(n-4)f[n+1] +2f[n] = 0.</math>

This example shows how problems generally solved using the power series solution method taught in normal differential equation classes can be solved in a much easier way.

'''Example:''' The differential equation

<math display="block">ay'' + by' +cy = 0</math>

has solution

<math display="block"> y=e^{ax}.</math>

The conversion of the differential equation to a difference equation of the Taylor coefficients is

<math display="block">af[n + 2] + bf[n + 1] + cf[n] = 0.</math>

It is easy to see that the <math>n</math>-th derivative of <math>e^{ax}</math> evaluated at <math>0</math> is <math>a^n</math>.

====Solving with z-transforms====
Certain difference equations - in particular, [[Z-transform#Linear constant-coefficient difference equation|linear constant coefficient]] difference equations - can be solved using [[z-transform]]s. The ''z''-transforms are a class of [[integral transform]]s that lead to more convenient algebraic manipulations and more straightforward solutions. There are cases in which obtaining a direct solution would be all but impossible, yet solving the problem via a thoughtfully chosen integral transform is straightforward.

====Solving with matrices====
Linear recurrences with constant coefficients can also be solved using matrix methods. For single roots of the characteristic polynomial, the [[Vandermonde matrix]] is useful.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kalman |first1=D. |date=1982 |title=Generalized Fibonacci Numbers by Matrix Methods |journal=The Fibonacci Quarterly |volume=20|issue=1 |pages=73-76 |doi=10.1080/00150517.1982.12430034  }}</ref> For multiple roots, the [[Vandermonde matrix#Confluent Vandermonde matrices|confluent Vandermonde matrix]] matrix is used.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sousa  |first1=A. |last2=Takayasu |first2=H.|last3=Takayasu |first3=M. |date=2019  |title=Random coefficient autoregressive processes and the PUCK model with fluctuating potential, Appendix A|journal= Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment |volume=013403 |pages=1-28 |doi=10.1088/1742-5468/aaf109  |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Stability==
In the solution equation

<math display="block">x_t = c_1\lambda_1^t +\cdots + c_n\lambda_n^t,</math>

a term with real characteristic roots converges to 0 as {{mvar|t}} grows indefinitely large if the absolute value of the characteristic root is less than 1. If the absolute value equals 1, the term will stay constant as {{mvar|t}} grows if the root is +1 but will fluctuate between two values if the root is −1. If the absolute value of the root is greater than 1 the term will become larger and larger over time. A pair of terms with complex conjugate characteristic roots will converge to 0 with dampening fluctuations if the absolute value of the modulus {{mvar|M}} of the roots is less than 1; if the modulus equals 1 then constant amplitude fluctuations in the combined terms will persist; and if the modulus is greater than 1, the combined terms will show fluctuations of ever-increasing magnitude.

Thus the evolving variable {{mvar|x}} will converge to 0 if all of the characteristic roots have magnitude less than 1. 

If the largest root has absolute value 1, neither convergence to 0 nor divergence to infinity will occur. If all roots with magnitude 1 are real and positive, {{mvar|x}} will converge to the sum of their constant terms {{math|''c''<sub>''i''</sub>}}; unlike in the stable case, this converged value depends on the initial conditions; different starting points lead to different points in the long run. If any root is −1, its term will contribute permanent fluctuations between two values. If any of the unit-magnitude roots are complex then constant-amplitude fluctuations of {{mvar|x}} will persist. 

Finally, if any characteristic root has magnitude greater than 1, then {{mvar|x}} will diverge to infinity as time goes to infinity, or will fluctuate between increasingly large positive and negative values.

A theorem of [[Issai Schur]] states that all roots have magnitude less than 1 (the stable case) [[if and only if]] a particular string of [[determinant]]s are all positive.<ref name=Baumol/>{{rp|p=247}}

If a non-homogeneous linear difference equation has been converted to homogeneous form which has been analyzed as above, then the stability and cyclicality properties of the original non-homogeneous equation will be the same as those of the derived homogeneous form, with convergence in the stable case being to the steady-state value {{math|''y''*}} instead of to 0.
